Item 1. Business

We design and sell industrial control equipment to original equipment manufacturers in North America, Europe and Asia.

Item 1A. Risk Factors

You should consider each of the following factors in evaluating our business and our prospects.

A failure of our information systems would interrupt our operations.

We depend on our own information systems, and on those our suppliers and logistics providers operate, to take orders, schedule production and ship product. An intrusion, a ransomware event or an extended outage would stop us taking and filling orders, and the cost of restoring the systems and of notifying the people whose data they hold could be material.

We buy the controller in our flagship product from a single supplier.

One supplier makes the motion controller used in every unit of our flagship product line, and it is manufactured at a single plant. If that plant stops producing, whether through equipment failure, a labour dispute or a natural disaster, we have no qualified second source and would be unable to ship the product line until a replacement part is designed, qualified and certified.

We may not realise what we expect from the businesses we buy.

We have acquired four businesses in the last five years and expect to acquire others. An acquisition can fail to earn what we paid for it because the products do not sell as we forecast, because the engineering teams do not stay, or because the accounting systems take longer to combine than we planned, and a shortfall would lead us to write down goodwill or other intangible assets.

We are a defendant in litigation that could result in substantial damages.

We are a defendant in patent litigation brought by a competitor in the Eastern District of Texas, and we are subject to other legal proceedings that arise in the ordinary course of our business. An adverse judgment, or a settlement on terms we do not now expect, could exceed the amounts we have accrued and would reduce our earnings in the period in which it is recorded.

Tariffs and trade restrictions raise our costs and can close a market.

We import components and export finished assemblies, and both are subject to tariffs, export licences and country of origin rules that governments change with little notice. A change that adds duty to a component we import, or that requires a licence to ship a finished assembly to a customer abroad, raises our cost or removes the sale altogether.

Three customers account for most of our revenue.

Our three largest customers together accounted for a majority of our revenue in each of the last three fiscal years, and none of them is obliged to buy any minimum quantity from us. A decision by any one of them to move a programme to a competitor, or to build the assembly in house, would reduce our revenue sharply and on short notice.

Our markets change faster than our development cycle.

The control systems our customers design into their equipment are replaced on a cycle shorter than the one on which we develop new products. If a generation of our products misses the design window for a customer programme, we do not get another opportunity at that programme until the following generation, which may be several years away.

Our credit agreement restricts what we may do with our cash.

Our revolving credit agreement contains a leverage covenant and an interest coverage covenant, each tested at the end of every fiscal quarter. A decline in earnings could put us out of compliance, and a waiver, if our lenders granted one at all, would come at a cost. If we could not obtain one, the lenders could accelerate the borrowings outstanding under the agreement.
